The model and posterior

Source: vignettes/model.Rmd
model.Rmd
library(retrogroup)

This vignette builds on vignette("framing", package = "retrogroup") and defines a Bayesian survival model to guide the reconstruction. Our goal is to construct the posterior probability of a patient belonging to a particular subgroup level given the observed survival data and treatment assignment. vignette("sampling", package = "retrogroup") uses estimates of these posterior probabilities to sample subgroup assignments for each patient. We begin by defining the hazard rate for a proportional hazards model, then write out the likelihood, derive the posterior probability of subgroup membership, and finally show how to estimate it.

Hazard rate

Along with the notation in vignette("framing", package = "retrogroup"), define:

  • \(x_i\): the unknown subgroup level of patient \(i\), a value in \(1, \ldots, K\). retrogroup seeks values of \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\) that are consistent with the published subgroup statistics from vignette("framing", package = "retrogroup").
  • \(t\) and \(z\): generic time and treatment indicator (1 for treatment, 0 for control), respectively.
  • \(\lambda_0(t)\): the baseline hazard rate at time \(t\), i.e. the hazard rate of a control patient (\(z = 0\)), which is the same for every subgroup level \(k\).

We define a proportional hazards model for the hazard rate, given a subgroup level \(k\) and treatment indicator \(z\):

\[ \lambda(t \mid k, z) := \lambda_0(t) \exp(\beta_k z) \]

We will also need the cumulative hazard, defined as:

\[ \Lambda(t \mid k, z) := \int_0^t \lambda(u \mid k, z) du \]

which simplifies to:

\[ \Lambda(t \mid k, z) = \exp(\beta_k z) \Lambda_0(t) \]

where the baseline cumulative hazard is defined as:

\[ \Lambda_0(t) := \int_0^t \lambda_0(u) du \]

Likelihood

We write the individual patient likelihood from Rodríguez (2010) in terms of the hazard rate above and survival function \(S(t \mid k, z)\). Unlike typical survival models, we have fixed values for \(\beta_k\), and the \(x_i\) values are the unknown parameters of interest.

\[ L(x_i \mid t_i, d_i, z_i) = \lambda(t_i \mid x_i, z_i)^{d_i} S(t_i \mid x_i, z_i) \]

Because \(S(t \mid k, z) = \exp(-\Lambda(t \mid k, z))\), we can express the likelihood in terms of the baseline hazard rate and baseline cumulative hazard:

\[ L(x_i \mid t_i, d_i, z_i) = \left[\lambda_0(t_i) \exp(\beta_{x_i} z_i)\right]^{d_i} \, \exp(-\Lambda_0(t_i) \exp(\beta_{x_i} z_i)) \]

This likelihood assumes that censoring is noninformative and does not depend on the subgroup level.

Posterior

Because treatment is randomized, \(x_i\) is independent of \(z_i\) a priori. Using prior \(\pi_k\) and likelihood \(L(k \mid t_i, d_i, z_i)\), Bayes’ Theorem gives the posterior probability that patient \(i\) belongs to subgroup level \(k\):

\[ P(x_i = k \mid t_i, d_i, z_i) = \frac{\pi_k L(k \mid t_i, d_i, z_i)}{\sum_{l=1}^K \pi_l L(l \mid t_i, d_i, z_i)} \]

For the prior of subgroup level \(k\), we use the published fraction of patients belonging to each subgroup level:

\[ \pi_k := \frac{n_k}{n} \]

Every \(\pi_k\) is strictly positive because vignette("framing", package = "retrogroup") requires \(n_k > 0\) for every subgroup level in the analysis.

Substituting in expressions for the likelihood and prior:

\[ P(x_i = k \mid t_i, d_i, z_i) = \frac{\frac{n_k}{n} \left[\lambda_0(t_i) \exp(\beta_k z_i)\right]^{d_i} \, \exp(-\Lambda_0(t_i) \exp(\beta_k z_i))}{\sum_{l=1}^K \frac{n_l}{n} \left[\lambda_0(t_i) \exp(\beta_l z_i)\right]^{d_i} \, \exp(-\Lambda_0(t_i) \exp(\beta_l z_i))} \]

The baseline hazard rate and total sample size cancel:

\[ P(x_i = k \mid t_i, d_i, z_i) = \frac{n_k \left[\exp(\beta_k z_i)\right]^{d_i} \, \exp(-\Lambda_0(t_i) \exp(\beta_k z_i))}{\sum_{l=1}^K n_l \left[\exp(\beta_l z_i)\right]^{d_i} \, \exp(-\Lambda_0(t_i) \exp(\beta_l z_i))} \]

Computation

The posterior probability above depends on the baseline cumulative hazard \(\Lambda_0(t)\), which is unknown. To estimate it, we use the control arm. Every control patient \(i\) has \(z_i = 0\) and therefore hazard rate \(\lambda_0(t)\) regardless of the unknown subgroup level \(x_i\). So the Nelson-Aalen estimator (Klein and Moeschberger 2003, sec. 4.2) applied to the control arm estimates \(\Lambda_0(t)\) directly:

\[ \hat{\Lambda}_0(t) := \sum_{i = 1}^n I(z_i = 0) \, I(t_i \le t) \, \frac{d_i}{\max(r_i, 1)} \]

where \(r_i\) is the number of control patients still at risk at time \(t_i\):

\[ r_i := \sum_{j = 1}^n I(z_j = 0) \, I(t_j \ge t_i) \]

Every control patient \(i\) has \(r_i \ge 1\), so \(\max(r_i, 1) = r_i\) in every term with \(I(z_i = 0) = 1\). A patient \(i\) with \(z_i = 1\) can have \(r_i = 0\), and the maximum keeps that term well defined, so terms with \(I(z_i = 0) = 0\) contribute zero to the sum. This estimator uses only the control arm events, so it gives up some precision in exchange for not depending on the unknown subgroup levels.

For each patient \(i\) and each potential subgroup level \(k\), we define a log-scale weight:

\[ w_{ik} := \log (n_k) + d_i \beta_k z_i - \hat{\Lambda}_0(t_i) \exp(\beta_k z_i) \]

We then define \(p_{ik}\) as our estimate of the posterior probability \(P(x_i = k \mid t_i, d_i, z_i)\), obtained by replacing \(\Lambda_0(t_i)\) with \(\hat{\Lambda}_0(t_i)\):

\[ p_{ik} := \frac{\exp(w_{ik})}{\sum_{l=1}^K \exp(w_{il})} \]

Every \(p_{ik}\) is strictly positive: because \(n_k > 0\), each \(w_{ik}\) is finite, so each \(\exp(w_{ik})\) is positive. In floating point arithmetic, a positive \(p_{ik}\) can still be numerically indistinguishable from zero, so retrogroup throws an error if any \(p_{ik}\) is less than the square root of machine epsilon.

Each \(p_{ik}\) is available in closed form. Its only inputs are the survival data and the published subgroup statistics from vignette("framing", package = "retrogroup"), and computing it requires no iteration or model fitting. These \(p_{ik}\) values are what vignette("sampling", package = "retrogroup") uses to sample subgroup assignments.

References

Klein, John P., and Melvin L. Moeschberger. 2003. Survival Analysis: Techniques for Censored and Truncated Data. 2nd ed. Statistics for Biology and Health. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/b97377.
Rodríguez, Germán. 2010. Parametric Survival Models. https://grodri.github.io/survival/ParametricSurvival.pdf.
